title: Installing IcomRigControl
subtitle: Getting the program onto your computer — Windows, macOS, Linux, or a Raspberry Pi.
in_this_chapter: Installer or portable — which to pick
Signed vs. unsigned: what you'll see

callout.label: In a nutshell
callout.text: Go to the official releases page, download the file for your computer, and run it. On Windows that is a Setup program; on macOS a disk image you drag into Applications; on Linux and the Raspberry Pi a package you install with one command. If your computer shows a one-time security caution, that is expected for now — this chapter tells you the exact clicks to get past it.

blocks.p: Always download IcomRigControl from its official releases page. Do not get it from anywhere else.

On that page, open the most recent release and look under **Assets** for the list of downloads. Each file is named for the computer it is for. Pick the one that matches yours from the table below, then follow the matching section.

rows: Windows / Mac / Linux PC or laptop (Intel or AMD)
Raspberry Pi or other ARM computer

callout.label: Not sure whether your Mac is Apple Silicon or Intel?
callout.text: Click the Apple menu at the top-left of the screen and choose **About This Mac**. If it says **Chip: Apple M1** (or M2, M3, M4), download the **arm64** file. If it says **Processor: Intel**, download the **x64** file.

blocks.h1: Installer or Portable — Which to Pick

blocks.p: Most downloads come in two forms, and you only need one:

bullets: **The installer** (the Setup program, the `.dmg`, or the `.deb`/`.rpm` package) is the simplest choice. It puts the program in the normal place, adds a menu shortcut, and can be uninstalled cleanly later. Pick this unless you have a reason not to.

**The portable archive** (a `.zip`) does not install anything — you unpack it to a folder and run the program in place. Handy for a USB stick or for trying it without touching the rest of your system.

steps: You may see one of two things — both are fine. If the build is **signed**, a **User Account Control** box may appear showing a verified publisher; click **Yes**. If instead you see **"Windows protected your PC,"** this copy is unsigned — click **More info**, then **Run anyway** (this is safe; see 'Signed vs. Unsigned' below).
The setup window opens. Click **Next** through the Welcome and License pages, leave the install folder at its default (`C:\Program Files\IcomRigControl`), and click **Install**.
When it finishes, click **Finish**. You now have an **IcomRigControl** shortcut on your Desktop and in the Start menu.

blocks.screenshot: Side by side: the signed User Account Control prompt showing the verified publisher, and the unsigned 'Windows protected your PC' prompt with the More info / Run anyway buttons

blocks.p: To remove it later: **Settings → Apps → IcomRigControl → Uninstall**, or use the Uninstall shortcut in the Start-menu folder.

steps: Download the Windows `.zip`, right-click it, choose **Extract All**, and pick a folder.
Open the extracted folder and double-click **`IcomRigControl.UI.exe`**. If a 'Windows protected your PC' prompt appears, click **More info → Run anyway**.
Download the disk image for your Mac — the **arm64** `.dmg` for Apple Silicon, or the **x64** `.dmg` for an Intel Mac.
Double-click the `.dmg` to open it. A window appears showing the **IcomRigControl** app and a shortcut to your **Applications** folder.

Open **Applications** and start IcomRigControl. If the build is **signed and notarized**, it opens normally (you may get a one-time 'downloaded from the Internet — are you sure you want to open it?' — click **Open**). If instead macOS says it **"cannot be opened because Apple cannot check it,"** this copy is unsigned — **right-click** (or Control-click) the app, choose **Open**, then click **Open** again. macOS remembers your choice and it opens normally afterward.

callout.label: The right-click step is only for an unsigned copy.
callout.text: A signed, notarized build opens with a normal double-click. The right-click → Open step is the standard one-time approval macOS asks for when a program is not signed. Apple signing for IcomRigControl is being set up; until it is finished, the Mac downloads are unsigned and you use the right-click → Open step once.

blocks.p: Unzip the archive. Then open **Terminal**, type `xattr -cr ` (with a trailing space), drag the unzipped folder into the Terminal window so its path fills in, and press **Return** — this clears the download-quarantine flag. Then run the `IcomRigControl.UI` program inside that folder.
First pick the download that matches your computer's processor:

bullets: **amd64 / x64** — a standard PC or laptop with an Intel or AMD processor.
**arm64 / aarch64** — a Raspberry Pi or other ARM-based computer.

callout.label: About the version number in these commands.
callout.text: The commands below show an example version like `1.0.0`. Type the exact name of the file you actually downloaded — your version number may differ. In a terminal you can type the first few letters of the file name and press **Tab** to complete the rest for you.

callout.label: Using a USB radio on Linux or macOS?
callout.text: Your user account must be allowed to open serial ports. On Linux, run `sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER`, then log out and back in. This is covered fully in the 'Connecting Your Radio Over USB' chapter.

steps: Install the **64-bit** Raspberry Pi OS (the tested version is 'Bookworm'). The 32-bit OS will not run IcomRigControl.
Download the **arm64** `.deb` and install it: `sudo dpkg -i icomrigcontrol_1.0.0_arm64.deb`.
Launch it from the application menu, or by running **`icomrigcontrol`** in a terminal.

callout.label: Headless (no-screen) Pi.
callout.text: You can also run the Pi with no monitor as a server sitting at the radio, controlled from your laptop or phone over the network. That uses the same `icomrigcontrol` command with extra options and is covered in the 'Remote / Network Mode' chapter.

blocks.h1: Signed vs. Unsigned: What You'll See

blocks.p: 'Code signing' is a digital seal that tells your computer who made a program and proves it has not been altered. When a program is signed, Windows and macOS trust it and show the author's name. When it is not, they show a one-time caution the first time you run it — not because anything is wrong, but because they cannot confirm the author automatically.

IcomRigControl's Windows builds are set up for code signing; macOS signing is being finished. Depending on the build and the date, a download may be **signed** or **unsigned**. Either way it is the identical program. Here is exactly what to expect and what to do.

headers: If the copy is unsigned — and what to do
rows: Installs normally; a User Account Control box may show a verified publisher — click Yes.
A 'Windows protected your PC' box appears. Click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. Safe — it only means this copy is not signed.
Opens with a normal double-click; you may get a one-time 'downloaded from the Internet — open?' — click Open.
macOS says it 'cannot be opened because Apple cannot check it.' **Right-click** (or Control-click) the app → **Open** → **Open**.
No warning — Linux does not gate apps this way.
No warning either; install and run normally.
